Local mirror refs/dotnet-docs/docs/fundamentals/syslib-diagnostics/syslib0060.md:35: "use ... RandomNumberGenerator.GetBytes ... to create a new array with cryptographically secure bytes"; the same page's sample is "byte[] salt = RandomNumberGenerator.GetBytes(saltSize);". Execution: two Hash calls on one password gave salts 7XoqLCV6ZazyxQLhBNx2ew== and BBI5LAqf/brA8kYD0MLuug==. The docs promise strength, not distinctness, which is why the claim's hedge ("not something any real run will produce") is the right wording.

API ref (net-10.0), FixedTimeEquals(ReadOnlySpan<Byte>, ReadOnlySpan<Byte>): "Determines the equality of two byte sequences in an amount of time that depends on the length of the sequences, but not their values." Remarks: "compares the contents from two buffers for equality in a way that doesn't leak timing information"; "will short-circuit and return false only if left and right have different lengths." Supports claim 6 and the round-3 section 4 wording "depends on the length ..., not on their contents".

No allowed source states PBKDF2 preimage resistance. Tried: (a) refs/dotnet-docs .../cryptographic-services.md:143 - only collision resistance ("it is computationally infeasible to find two distinct inputs that hash to the same value"); (b) grep of all of refs/ for "irreversib|one-way|preimage" - no cryptography hit; (c) refs/aspnetcore-docs password-hashing.md - describes calling Pbkdf2, nothing about reversal. Nearest allowed line, CA5387, speaks of "dictionary attacks that try to guess" - guessing, not inversion. The lesson already uses round 1's suggested wording, so no new issue.

refs/dotnet-docs/docs/fundamentals/code-analysis/quality-rules/security-warnings.md:98 (CA5387): "This rule checks if a cryptographic key was generated by Rfc2898DeriveBytes with an iteration count of less than 100,000. A higher iteration count can help mitigate against dictionary attacks that try to guess the generated cryptographic key." Measured on dotnet 10, Pbkdf2 / SHA256 / 32-byte output, same salt: 10,000 iterations 10 ms; 100,000 iterations 103 ms; 1,000,000 iterations 1037 ms — proportional, as claimed.

issues.text: Two small gaps in the new sentence pair. (a) The early-exit behaviour of 'an ordinary comparison' is not in the ledger: claim 6 only covers FixedTimeEquals itself; no allowed doc states that ordinary comparisons stop at the first differing byte (the API remarks only say FixedTimeEquals 'doesn't leak timing information'). (b) Placed right after 'not `==`', it reads as if `==` is that byte-by-byte comparison; for byte[] `==` is reference equality (C# docs: 'reference-type operands ... are equal if they refer to the same object'), so it would not compare contents at all.
issues.quote: not `==` — a comparison whose duration depends on the length of the two byte sequences, not on their contents. An ordinary comparison can stop at the first byte that differs
issues.fix: Replace 'not `==`' with 'not a plain byte-by-byte comparison'. Extend claim 6 text to: '...not on where or whether they first differ; a plain byte-by-byte comparison may stop at the first differing byte, which is the timing information FixedTimeEquals avoids leaking.' (kind: behavior, version_key: dotnet, source_hint: API ref CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals Remarks).
